name: Bilal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we do not sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a usual working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Bilal Gupta, 43, and I do general carpentry and labouring on building sites. My partner and two school-age children live with me; I start by checking my pencil and tape, then carry boards and help the carpenter set frames.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which part of the day do you enjoy, and which part takes the most out of you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a frame sits square and the room finally looks like a room. The lifting wears me out, and I still need someone to check my cut before it goes into place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker order list is useful only when the boards are right. I still want a person who knows the job to look at the material before we cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mostly carry, measure and fit things, so a small office change does not seem likely to replace my main tasks. I worry about money already because less than a month of savings is not much against a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the days the supervisor offers and ask about next week before I leave. If pay came in short, I would mend my work gloves again rather than buy another pair straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small software change does not frighten me on the job. What gets to me is an empty week on the board when the mortgage still needs paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check before cutting a board for a frame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mark it with my pencil and look at the tape again before I cut. A straight cut counts more than a faster note when the board is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and your partner do when work is slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We look at the bills due and decide what can wait without causing trouble. The children’s everyday needs come first, and we do not have much room for extras.

say: I would say **a correct order list** matters more than speed.
I would want **a skilled person** to check the boards before we cut.
think: I mostly do **hands-on work**, so a small office change seems limited for me.
I have **thin savings**, and the mortgage is already a pressure.
do: Keep taking **offered site days** and ask about next week before leaving.
Mend my **work gloves** again if pay comes in short.
feel: **This change** does not frighten me at work, but an empty week worries me.
S0.quote: A straight cut counts more than a faster note when the board is wrong.
fieldNote: He separates modest office efficiency from the **physical work** he does.
**Thin savings** make the mortgage a present concern even in a mild scenario.
He and his partner defer **non-urgent purchases** when pay is short.

steps.text: Keep taking offered site days and ask about next week before leaving
Mend work gloves again before buying replacements during a short-pay week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can use its new system, but the site still needs someone who understands the cut. I would rather ask a carpenter than follow a screen if the marks do not line up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI now, and a new screen would take me longer than someone younger who already knows it. If the office changes its notes, I could lose some small tasks, but I cannot say that means fewer whole building jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to keep showing me the current plan on paper until I have seen the new process work. I would continue with fitting and carrying jobs, and I would ask the carpenter to check my measurements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy about being slower with a screen when I am already the junior worker. I would try to learn if someone stood beside me, but I would not pay for a class from money needed at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you willing to try the new process?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to see it used on one real site order before I trusted it. If it gives the same result as the paper plan and the carpenter agrees, I could try the next one with help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work would you ask the carpenter to keep checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask him to check the measurements before I cut a frame. I know I can miss a small mark when I am trying to hurry, and I would rather ask than waste timber.

say: I would say **the site needs judgement** even when the office uses a new system.
I would ask a carpenter when screen marks **do not line up**.
think: I do not use AI now, and a **new screen** would take me longer to learn.
I could lose small note tasks, but I do not know if **whole site jobs** would fall.
do: Ask the supervisor to keep showing me the **current plan** until I understand the new process.
Continue **fitting and carrying** while asking the carpenter to check measurements.
feel: I feel **uneasy about being slower**, but I would learn with someone beside me.
S1.quote: I would not pay for a class from money needed at home.
fieldNote: His **technology resistance** makes a supported demonstration more plausible than self-study.
He avoids assuming office changes reduce **whole building jobs**.
His **low skill level** makes careful measurement checks important to him.

steps.text: Keep current fitting and carrying work while the new process is demonstrated
Wait to use the new process until its site result is checked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI takes the thinking tasks first, and the robot part comes later. I would not call those years protection, because no one has promised me work until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may do the measurements and planning notes I sometimes help with by 2028. I could still be carrying boards for a time, but robots may take that work too, and I do not have enough savings to wait without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028, I would ask the carpenter to teach me how he checks a frame for level before fixing it. In 2029, I would take paid site work when I can and keep the mortgage money ahead of new tool purchases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not much time for someone still learning the basics. I can ask for help and practise, but I cannot promise the work will last or cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner notice first if your pay fell in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would see me checking the schedule more often and putting off things we had planned to replace. I would tell them the money is short before we missed a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can the three years before robots arrive do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can give me time to learn more of the physical work if a carpenter has time to teach. They do not give me a guaranteed place on a crew, so I would still ask about shifts.

say: I would say **thinking tasks go first**, with robots coming later.
I would not call the delay **protection** when no one promises work until 2031.
think: I think AI may do **measurement and planning notes** by 2028.
I do not have **enough savings to wait** without pay if robots take the physical work.
do: Ask the carpenter to teach me **frame level** checks before 2028.
Keep mortgage money ahead of **new tool purchases** in 2029.
Take available **paid shifts** on site during 2029.
feel: **Two years** is not much time for someone still learning the basics.
I can practise, but cannot promise **my pay** will cover the bills.
S2.quote: I do not have enough savings to wait without pay.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **thinking tasks by 2028** from the later robot threat.
His **2029 plan** protects the mortgage before new tool spending.
He does not assume the robot delay means **guaranteed work**.

steps.text: Learn how to check a frame for level with the carpenter before 2028
Delay new tool purchases in 2029 to keep mortgage money available
Take available paid site shifts during 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives me time to practise a better cut and learn how the crew sets a frame. I would not say that means the work is safe after the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take the schedules and measurement notes I help with by 2031. Robots arrive around 2034 and may take on the carrying too, so I would need to be ready for work to change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the carpenter to let me fit a frame with him checking each step over the next few years. In 2032, I would find out whether local builders need that skill before I spent money on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a useful stretch to learn, but not a reason to wait until the last minute. My savings are thin, so I would need each practice day to be paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would you want the carpenter to catch while you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes rush the measurement when the crew is waiting. I would ask him to check that first, because correcting the mark is easier than removing a frame later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before paying for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which local builders use the skill and whether they hire for it now. If all I hear is a promise that jobs may come, I would wait and keep practising on site.

say: I would say **five years** gives me time to practise a better cut and learn frame setting.
I would not say that makes work **safe after robots arrive**.
think: I think AI could take **scheduling notes** by 2031.
I would prepare for **another change in 2034** when robots could take on carrying.
do: Ask the carpenter to coach me while I **fit a frame** over the next few years.
Wait to pay for a course in 2032 until **local hiring** is clear.
feel: **Five years** gives me time to learn without waiting until the last minute.
I need practice to be paid because **my savings are thin**.
S3.quote: I would say five years gives me time to practise a better cut and learn how the crew sets a frame.
fieldNote: He identifies **measurement errors** as a practical skill to improve.
He will wait on course costs until builders confirm **current hiring needs**.
**Paid practice** matters because household savings cannot support a long pause.

steps.text: Practise fitting frames with the carpenter checking each step
Wait on a course until local builders confirm hiring needs in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a long warning gives families room to talk and prepare. I would not call any trade safe, because robots still arrive in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes and planning I sometimes help with could be done by AI in 2036, and robots could reach site jobs in 2039. My children will be older by then and may need a different kind of support from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep learning the carpentry tasks the crew needs while someone can show me how to do them. In 2037, I would talk with my partner and our children about what the older one wants to study when that choice is closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me a chance to see whether builders are still hiring and to improve some skills. The mortgage is due now too, and I cannot plan as if all the money worries wait until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your children’s plans for school today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would wait until the older child is choosing subjects and listen to what they want. We can talk through the choices then instead of steering them toward the work I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that two years did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a task over several seasons and watch what builders ask their crews to do. I would still have to make decisions about the mortgage and the children as life changes, not only about machines.

say: I would say **a decade** gives families room to prepare.
I would not call **any trade safe** while robots still arrive.
think: I think AI could do **notes and planning** by 2036, with robots reaching site jobs in 2039.
**My children** will be older, and may need different support from us.
do: Keep learning **carpentry tasks** the crew needs while someone can teach me.
Discuss **study choices** with my partner and older child when they are closer.
feel: **Ten years** gives me a chance to improve and watch local hiring.
I cannot set aside today’s **mortgage worries** until 2039.
S4.quote: I cannot plan as if all the money worries wait until 2039.
fieldNote: He values **time to prepare** without calling any trade safe.
He leaves the child’s study decision until **that choice is closer**.
His **children’s future needs** may differ from current household costs.

steps.text: Learn more carpentry tasks through supervised site practice
Discuss the older child’s study plans with the family in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it leaves little time to improve or build our savings. Steady paid shifts and a carpenter who teaches me properly would help more than a screen or a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want to keep learning a trade I can do well, but I still need someone to show me where I am going wrong. My family counts on this month’s pay, so a long warning does not settle tonight’s bills.

theadlineQuote: My family counts on this month’s pay, so a long warning does not settle tonight’s bills.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid teaching** and steady shifts would help more than borrowing for a course.
portrait: Bilal is a **43-year-old junior construction worker** supporting his partner and two school-age children.
His **thin savings** make even a short site closure difficult.
He prefers **trusted hands-on teaching** over unfamiliar screens.
He values **steady trade work**, but does not assume robots leave it safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives him little time to improve or build savings.
headlineQuote: My family counts on this month’s pay, so a long warning does not settle tonight’s bills.
